1:
Robertson objects to the page rather than the text: there is no break in the argument on the psalm, and this is a poor chapter division. Ellicott places the stress within the sentence — on fear, not on us — and notes that the writer begins with let us though about to write lest any of you, having gained his object if he brings his readers to share his fear. Calvin makes it a rule of pastoral care, that a good shepherd so watches the flock that no one sheep is lost, and every one ought to fear for his neighbours as well as himself; but he fences the word at once, since the fear recommended is not that which shakes the confidence of faith but such as keeps us from growing torpid with indifference. Henry reads the promise as a legacy left us by Christ in his last will and testament, so that our business is to see that we be the legatees; and he argues from strength, that the best privileges the ancient Jews had were their gospel privileges, since whatever was excellent in the sacrifices was their respect to Christ.

The word rendered seem is the first real difficulty, and no two of them treat it alike. Clarke passes over it, taking the clause to mean lest any of us should actually come short, that is, miss it. Ellicott holds it impossible that the sense can be should even seem, or should think himself to have failed; the writer may be avoiding direct language about what lies beyond mortal ken, but more probably he is drawn on by the figure in the next word, the falling short of a mark, and so refers to the judge who declares the failure — lest any one be adjudged to have come short. Calvin reports that some consider the word pleonastic and grants it sometimes is, but holds it has a special meaning here, the Apostle wishing no one to present even the appearance of neglecting the promised rest; and Henry sharpens that into a warning, that it is a dreadful thing so much as to seem to fall short. Clarke hears in the verb an allusion to the Grecian games, of which this epistle has many: he that came short was any distance, no matter how small, behind the winner — and will it avail us how near we get to heaven, if the door be shut before we arrive?

The second verse turns on a variant. Clarke reports that several of the best copies read the participle as agreeing not with the word but with the people, so that the sense becomes they were not mixed with those who heard it by faith, not of the same spirit with Joshua and Caleb; though he judges the common text best. Ellicott says the change of reading rests on the strongest authority and compels us to connect the words with the people rather than the message, so that speakers and hearers must be united by the bond of faith. Robertson calls the phrase very difficult and leaves the text uncertain, observing only that on the reading which agrees with the people the translation is correct. Clarke explains the metaphor by the nutrition of the body, since food received into the stomach and not mixed with the saliva and the gastric juice would be the means of death rather than life; and he supports the usage from a description of health as a proper mixture of the wet and dry, the cold and hot. Calvin draws the doctrine instead: the word separated from faith can confer no good — not that its power depends on us, for were the whole world false he who cannot lie would still be true, but it never puts forth its power in us except when faith gives it entrance.
3:
Calvin begins with a claim about method: the writer has hitherto taken the psalm according to the letter, but now amplifies and decorates it, so that he rather alludes to than explains the words of David — an embellishment Paul had used before on a saying of Moses, and nothing unsuitable when Scripture is accommodated to the subject in hand. Ellicott states the aim more soberly, that the object is not to establish a truth absolutely new but to show that in this Scripture and in that a received truth lies contained. Robertson will not soften it at all: the perfect tense carries the permanent value of what was said, God has spoken, and that is enough for us. On the opening clause Ellicott finds the emphasis two-fold, on believed, which looks back to the faith of the previous verse, and on we enter, which looks forward; the purport being that the rest exists and that entering into it may still be spoken of.

What that rest is, and whether it is had now, divides them. Gill denies it is eternal rest, which all believers shall enjoy but do not now, and makes it spiritual rest in Christ under the Gospel dispensation — a rest from the burden of the law and from all toil for salvation by works, lying in much inward peace notwithstanding the world's troubles. Clarke agrees that we actually possess it, having peace of conscience and joy in the Holy Ghost and being saved from the guilt and power of sin, these blessings being the forerunners of the eternal glory typified by the earthly felicity promised to Israel. Robertson takes the present tense as emphatic and futuristic — we are sure to enter in, we who believe. Calvin looks furthest forward, defining the true rest of the faithful, which is to continue for ever, as the state in which they shall rest as God did, since the highest happiness of man is to be united to his God. Clarke reports the textual state of the clause: the words we who believe are omitted by Chrysostom and a few copies, and several others read therefore let us enter rather than for we do enter, which would answer neatly to therefore let us fear in the first verse; but that reading cannot stand, since the words it requires to be dropped are acknowledged genuine by every manuscript of note.

The two short verses that follow are treated as scaffolding rather than argument. Calvin calls them explanatory of the sentence before and parenthetic, and lays out what each stage of the reasoning turns on: the word rest, to show the rest meant was not the Sabbath, and then the word to day, to show it was not the rest of Canaan. Wesley states the same chain as a bare proof — the psalm mentions a rest, but not God's rest from creating, since that was long before the time of Moses, so that in his time another rest was expected, of which those who then heard fell short. Ellicott adds why the caution was needed, that the psalmist's words are drawn from the opening of Genesis, so that though the same words are used the thought is widely different. Barnes generalises rather than argues, finding the notion of rest running through every dispensation, seen in the finishing of creation, in the appointment of the Sabbath, in the offer of the promised land and now in the promise of heaven; and he is careful that God's resting does not mean he was wearied, only that he ceased from creation while never ceasing to carry forward the affairs of the universe. Robertson notes that a Jewish writer quotes the same verse with the same mannerism of indefinite citation, and that the seventh day of God's rest was still going on, and so was clearly not a day of twenty-four hours.
6:
Clarke opens with the chapter's sharpest attack, on the translators. He cannot conjecture why they inserted the word must, and hopes it was not to serve a system, since some have since used it so — some must go to heaven, for so is the doctrine of the decree, and certain persons must be infallibly brought thither as a reward to Christ for his sufferings, in which the will of man has no part. Supposing all that true, he says, it is not in the text either positively or by implication; literally rendered it says only that it remaineth for some to enter in. Barnes, without noticing the quarrel, builds the argument Clarke suspects: it was a settled matter that some would enter, since a rest deserving to be called the rest of God would not be prepared in vain, and as those to whom it was first offered would not enter, it must have been designed for others. Ellicott summarises the five particulars the preceding verses establish and finds them repeated here; and he notices that this verse says disobedience where the second said unbelief, comparing the transition elsewhere from believeth to obeyeth. Robertson makes an admission the others do not: the argument is rabbinical throughout, though the author is writing to Jews.

On the certain day the voices converge. Barnes explains the verb as bounding a field and then fixing definitely, so that the writer mentions to day particularly; the object being to show the offer was not confined to those who first received it, since five hundred years later David still speaks of a rest that might be lost by hardening the heart. Clarke reaches the same end by another road: the day of rest for the ancient Jews being past and the true rest never enjoyed, God in mercy has instituted another day, so that his voice is in the Gospel as it was in the law. Ellicott takes in David to mean the Book of Psalms, though the Greek version ascribes this psalm to him; Robertson says the same. Calvin alone states the objection before answering it: David's words seem to express no such thing, meaning only that God punished the people's unbelief by refusing them the land. His answer is that the inference holds, for if nothing were promised now the warning would be unsuitable — take heed lest the same thing happen to you as to the fathers — so that as their unbelief deprived them, the promise is renewed to their children.

The last verse turns on a name, and all agree what it is. Clarke calls it truly surprising that the translators wrote Jesus and not Joshua, since the Greek version everywhere renders the Hebrew name so, and it is that reading the apostle follows. One manuscript adds the son of Nave to prevent the wrong application, that Theodoret and a Syriac version do the same, and that Coverdale and Tindal and later English editions read Joshua, as does our own margin — a pity it was not in the text, since the smaller Bibles carry no margin and simple people are bewildered by it. Barnes says there can be no doubt Joshua is intended, and states what the name serves to prove: Joshua did give them a rest in the land, but not all that was intended, and had it been final the matter would not have been alluded to again in David's time. Ellicott and Robertson agree, Robertson adding that the conditional assumes its condition unfulfilled, and correcting the English tense. Gill turns aside to draw out the type — the agreement in the names, both signifying a saviour, the one temporal and the other spiritual; both servants in office; and the correspondence in the battles won, the saving of Rahab, the receiving of the Gibeonites, and the leading of Israel into Canaan to divide it by lot.
9:
The conclusion arrives, and the word it arrives at is a new one. Barnes observes that the noun here is not the ordinary word for a Sabbath but a word meaning the keeping of one, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament, and he rules out the alternatives in turn: it cannot mean the rest in Canaan, since the whole drift has been to prove otherwise; it cannot mean the Sabbath proper, or the usual word would have been used; it cannot mean the Christian Sabbath, or the reasoning about being excluded by unbelief would be irrelevant. It must therefore mean heaven, and the best description of heaven is to call it an eternal Sabbath — a place where there will be employment without fatigue, where the slave shall rest from his toil and the man broken by anxious care shall cease from his labours. Gill takes the opposite view of the same rest, denying that eternal rest is meant at all, since that is not entered now and cannot be laboured for, salvation not being by works; the Gospel rest is intended, which believers enter by degrees and enjoy more of by believing. Clarke declines to choose and says he understands it as including both.

The tenth verse produces the sharpest division in the chapter, over who is meant. Gill argues it is not believers but Christ himself, on the grounds that a single person is spoken of and not many, that the rest entered is his own, which can be said of no other, and that the comparison with God's ceasing from his works fits only him — so that Christ entered his rest not when laid in the grave but when he rose and sat down at the right hand of God, and that is the ground of the saints' rest. Clarke reads it of the believer, who has ceased from his own works in the sense of no longer depending on Mosaic rites for justification, resting from them as fully as God rested from creation. Ellicott reads it the same way and adds the symmetry: as God's rest was the goal of the creative work, so this rest is the goal of the life of works for the people of God. He then raises the question the whole argument has been inviting — how far this wide meaning is present in the psalm itself — and answers it flatly, that we have no right to look on the argument of this section as an accommodation or a mere application of Scripture, since the psalmist's language, which pointedly changes the historian's words about the land into words about God's rest, was susceptible of the higher meaning already.

The exhortation that closes the section is read as effort against presumption. Chrysostom states the principle without softening it: faith is great and brings salvation, and without it none can be saved, but it suffices not of itself, there being need of a right conversation also — and if those who suffered such distress in the wilderness were not counted worthy of the land, how shall we be counted worthy of heaven if we live carelessly? Clarke takes the verb to imply every exertion of body and mind, all other things omitted that this one thing be done, and draws the conclusion his system requires: the apostle never supposed a man might not make final shipwreck of faith so long as he was in a state of probation. Calvin keeps the figure rather than the doctrine, noting that entering into rest is compared to a straight course and falling set in opposition to it, so that the metaphor continues through both clauses. Robertson explains the last noun as meaning a copy, and adds the plain moral: the Israelites set a terrible example, and it is so easy to copy the bad ones.
12:
Whether the word here is Christ or the Scripture is the chapter's great dispute, unusual in that the commentators name their sides. A note in Calvin's text sets out the roll: the fathers and later divines are divided, Augustin and Ambrose and Owen and Doddridge holding it to be Christ, Chrysostom and Theophylact and Beza holding it to be Scripture — the latter clearly the most suitable, the only difficulty being the verse that follows, where a transition is made from the word of God to God himself. Gill takes the other side. It is Christ, the essential Word; the Word of God was a known name of the Messiah among the Jews, which is why the apostle uses it in writing to them; not a thing but a person is spoken of, a Judge and critical discerner of the secrets of men's hearts, who is said to be a priest in the verses following. Clarke argues against him on a single ground of usage: Paul in none of his thirteen acknowledged epistles so denominates our Lord, nor does any New Testament writer except John. Owen attempted the contrary, he grants, but his two supporting texts fail. He then quotes Calmet, who concedes that none of the properties named here can be denied to the Son — he sees all things, penetrates all things, rules the heart and turns it where he pleases — yet denies the Logos is intended, since the conjunction shows the verse is an inference from what precedes about rest.

Ellicott states both cases before deciding. Outside John's writings, he grants, no passage invests the word of God so clearly with personal attributes; there certainly is personification, and the language would, standing alone, suggest a divine Person. But he cannot believe the phrase sharper than a two-edged sword would be applied directly to the Son, and this epistle refers repeatedly to the word of God in revelation with no trace of another meaning; the key is its habitual thought of Scripture as a direct divine utterance. He therefore takes it as the whole word of God, mainly of threatening but also of promise. He is careful about the Alexandrian parallels: the resemblances to Philo, who speaks of the divine Word cutting through all things and separating the parts of the soul, are too close to be accidental, but prove familiarity rather than adoption of his system. Robertson puts the same judgement in a line: the author uses Philonic language rather than Philonic ideas. Barnes declines the question, taking the word of God as what God speaks, promise or threatening, law or gospel, and reading the verse for its purpose, that we cannot escape God's notice.

On the imagery they converge. Barnes and Robertson both note that the adjective means two-mouthed, Barnes explaining that the sword was given a mouth because it seemed to devour what was before it, and that the Roman sword was commonly two-edged, which made it easier to penetrate and to cut every way. Ellicott insists on a rendering that changes the sense: it divides soul and spirit, not soul from spirit, severing bone from bone and piercing the marrow, the words transferred by a natural metaphor from the material frame to the soul. Calvin asks a question none of the others put: whether the effect described belongs to all hearers or only to the faithful. His answer is that it must be confined to the faithful, since only they are searched to the quick, hypocrisy sifted and the old man slain by the edge of the spiritual sword — and yet the context shows a general truth, for the reprobate, though they set an iron heart against it, are dragged to the tribunal by the very word they deride, like furious dogs that bite and claw the chain by which they are bound and can do nothing.
13:
One participle divides them further than anything else here, and each canvasses the options before choosing. Wesley takes it as sacrificial, alluding to the victims under the law, first flayed and then laid open. Clarke reports it in full — the beast slain, flayed and so naked, cut open so that the intestines are exposed, inspected by the priest lest an imperfect offering be made, and split so exactly down the chine that the spinal marrow was cloven down the centre — but suspects it is not the metaphor here, since the verb signifies to have the neck bent back so as to expose the face, as was often done with criminals that they might be the better recognised; and he supports it from a panegyric before an emperor, where the informers' upturned faces and twisted necks are a public spectacle. Barnes dismisses both: the sacrificial derivation he calls manifestly forced, and the criminal reading, first proposed by Erasmus and adopted by Clarke, equally forced and unnatural; and he reports a third view, that the allusion is to cutting the animal down the back-bone, which Bloomfield adopted claiming the authority of Chrysostom and Grotius and Beza, though it is not in fact the sentiment of Grotius, who supposed the skin stripped off by dividing it at the neck. His own answer is that the simplest sense is usually best: the word relates to the neck, not the marrow or the skin, and means to bend the neck back so as to expose it when an animal is slain. The allusion is therefore to the sword of the previous verse, and we are like a beast whose neck is bent back and laid bare, with nothing to hinder the stroke.

Ellicott declines to settle it: the word is peculiar and the exact metaphor cannot be determined with certainty. It is usually applied to a wrestler who overthrows his adversary by dragging back the neck, so prostrate has been suggested; the criminal explanation is attested in Latin authors but not for the Greek word; and there is no good reason, he says, to suppose an allusion to a sacrificial victim at all. Robertson adds a sixth picture, the verb meaning to bend back the neck as the surgeon does for operating, and glosses the verse with a figure of his own — God's microscope can lay bare the smallest microbe of doubt and sin, and there are no mental reservations from God.

The closing phrase is disputed too, and Calvin is sharpest about it. He holds the conjunction causal, the argument drawn from the nature of God himself: nothing is so deep in man's soul that it cannot be drawn into light by the word that resembles its own author. Interpreters, he says, have strangely perverted the passage for want of seeing that God's word is like a long staff by which he searches what lies deep in our hearts; and the ambiguity of the last words has led them astray too, since they render them of whom we speak when they ought to be rendered with whom we have to do — so that we should not trifle with him as with a mortal man but tremble whenever his word is set before us. Barnes reads the phrase as an account to be settled, and turns it into a thought experiment: were we transparent, so that the world could see all we are, who would dare go abroad? The gay multitudes in the streets would become processions of downcast and blushing convicts. Gill keeps the Christological reading of the previous verse and applies the omniscience to Christ, creature being often used by the Rabbins for man. Ellicott records a division of another kind: following Luther, both Tyndale and Coverdale begin the fifth chapter at the verse after this one, but the connection with what precedes is too close to justify it.
14:
Whether this verse concludes or begins comes first. Clarke reports that the particle we translate seeing should be rendered now, since the apostle, though he had called Christ a high priest twice already, does not attempt to prove it in any preceding chapter but enters on the point here and pursues it for six chapters; and he offers a second possibility, that the words resume a discourse broken off earlier, all that intervenes being a parenthesis, since the argument then runs on with perfect connection. Calvin holds the opposite, that an inference is employed, the writer having referred to this truth before; and he supplies why the two offices belong together, that the Son sustained a twofold character when sent to us, teacher and priest, the design of both being to enable us to come to God. Ellicott finds all the chief points of the earlier chapters gathered here — the high priesthood, the exaltation, the divine Sonship, the compassion toward the brethren whose lot he came to share. Robertson maps the whole book from this verse, Jesus having been shown superior to the prophets, to angels and to Moses, and now to the Levitical line; and he sets out the five points still to come, a better priest, a better covenant, a better sanctuary, a better sacrifice and better promises. Gill draws the thread back rather than forward: this great high priest is no other than the Word of God just spoken of, and he notes that Philo often calls the divine Word a priest and a high priest.

Two smaller points divide them. Barnes explains the epithet great from Jewish usage, since in the apostle's time the name belonged also to the deputy, to those who had held the office and retired, and perhaps to the head of each of the twenty-four courses, so that great high priest designates the man actually at the head. On the participle, Ellicott corrects the English: it is not passed into the heavens but passed through them, as the high priest passed through the Holy Place to enter the Holy of Holies, and Robertson agrees, taking Jesus through the upper heavens up to the throne where he performs his office. Barnes keeps the simpler picture of entrance, the Jewish high priest going once a year into the most holy place while the Christian High Priest has gone into heaven to sprinkle the blood of atonement. Clarke supplies the objection the whole passage answers, put by those Jews who wished the Christians of Palestine to apostatize: you have no tabernacle, no temple, no high priest, no sacrifice.

On the sympathy itself Clarke narrows what the others widen, and the difference matters. Barnes takes it broadly: our High Priest is not cold and unfeeling but was subjected to every kind of trial we can face, persecuted, poor, despised, enduring the sorrows of a cruel death; had he been cold, his stateliness would only awe us and his distance repel us. Ellicott presses further, that he does not merely show compassion to the suffering but takes to himself a joint feeling of their weaknesses, and that the word must not be limited to pain and bodily suffering but covers whatever belongs to the necessary limitations of the nature he assumed. Clarke agrees that Christ sympathizes with our weakness, but adds a restriction none of the others make: his body was perfectly tempered and free from all morbid action, and his human soul, being every way perfect, could feel no irregular temper — in these respects he was different from us, and cannot as man sympathize with us in any feelings of that kind, though as God he has provided support for the body and an atoning sacrifice for the soul. Ellicott adds a note of another sort, that the beautiful rendering touched with the feeling of our infirmities is owed to a sixteenth-century testament.
16:
Clarke keeps the day of atonement in view and reads the throne as its answering piece. The approach is to the propitiatory, the covering of the ark of the testimony with a cherub at each end and between them the symbol of the Divine Majesty; and the superiority of the new covenant over the old lies in who may come. There the high priest only was permitted to approach, with fear and trembling and not without the blood of the victim, and if he transgressed he might expect to be struck with death; here all may approach who feel their need, with freedom and liberty of speech in opposition to that fear. Barnes builds on the same picture, God seated on the mercy-seat while the great High Priest, having shed his own blood, pleads for the pardon of men, so that we come not on our own merits but where a sufficient sacrifice has been offered. Whom they come to is disputed. Gill offers both readings, either to Christ, typified by the mercy seat, or else to the Father, since Christ is the way of access; Robertson takes it of the high priest, so that instead of deserting him we make daily use of him; Calvin makes it access to God, open to all who come relying on Christ the Mediator.

What is asked for divides them more sharply. Barnes puts pardon first, since we are guilty and self-condemned and our first cry should be for mercy, and he who comes without feeling his need of it must fail of the divine favour; grace comes second, the strength needed even by the forgiven, to keep them from sin in temptation. Clarke divides them the same way, mercy referring to the pardon of sin and grace to what supports the soul afterwards; and as Christ tasted death for every man, every man may go to that propitiatory and take mercy suited to his degree of guilt. Ellicott denies the premise: the real meaning is to receive compassion in our weakness and trials, and the thought of obtaining mercy for guilt is not in these words taken by themselves, though grace meets every need. The previous verse having shown that our High Priest knows what help is required, this one assures us it will be given in the time of need.

The closing phrase draws out the best of them. Clarke works the etymology of the word for help, which signifies to run at the cry, and turns it into a rule: no help can be expected where there is no cry, and where there is no cry there is no felt necessity, for he that feels he is perishing cries aloud, and to such a cry the compassionate High Priest runs. Nor is the timing indifferent: we are not to cry to day to be helped to morrow, or at the hour of death, but to call when we need mercy and grace and to expect them when we call. Robertson catches the same word in a phrase, help in the nick of time, and takes boldness to mean telling Jesus the whole story of our shortcomings. Calvin turns the verse into a controversy. The chief benefit of divine teaching is a sure confidence in calling on God, and religion falls to the ground when that certainty is taken from consciences; so he holds the light of the Gospel extinct where men are bidden to doubt whether God is propitious, and where Christ is confessed a Mediator in words while the power of his priesthood is made of none effect by the anxious seeking of other mediators. His comfort is in the name the throne is given: it is not arrayed in naked majesty to confound us, for God's glory contemplated alone could only fill us with despair, but is adorned with grace, a name that allures us by its sweetness.
